CHENNAI: The TVK govt on Monday announced a Rs 20,800-crore project to establish a 1,600MW new supercritical thermal power station in Tuticorin, along with a Rs 33,066-crore plan to overhaul Tamil Nadu’s power transmission network.Making the announcements under Rule 110 in the Assembly, chief minister C Joseph Vijay said the state needed world-class power infrastructure to meet its growing economy and rising electricity demand.The proposed Tuticorin project will comprise two 800MW units and will be implemented under the public-private partnership (PPP) model.The new facility will gradually replace the existing five 210MW coal-fired units at the Tuticorin thermal power station, which have been commissioned in phases since 1979.“To effectively handle the continuously increasing power load and meet the growing demand, investments in the power generation sector are essential,” Vijay said.The govt said TN’s renewable energy capacity, including wind and solar power, was expanding rapidly, but generation from these sources was not available uniformly through the day.While battery storage capacity was being developed to store surplus renewable power for use during peak periods, thermal generation would continue to be required to ensure uninterrupted supply during periods of high demand.The transmission overhaul will include 196 new substations and 15,000km of new transmission lines, besides strengthening existing networks to evacuate power from generating stations to major consumption centres such as Chennai.For Chennai’s distribution network, the govt announced Rs 1,762 crore worth of works, including 36 new 33/11kV substations, new distribution transformers and replacement of ageing cables, conductors, pillar boxes and circuit breakers.“A comprehensive power infrastructure equipped with advanced technology is essential for Tamil Nadu’s growing economy and increasing power consumption,” the chief minister said.
Article Summary: The TVK announced a Rs 20,800-crore project to establish a 1,600MW new supercritical power station in Tuticorin. Tamil Nadu’s transmission overhaul will include 196 new substations and 15,000km of new transmission lines. Chief minister C Joseph Vijay said the state needed world-class power infrastructure to meet its growing economy.

Article Title: How 60-year-old India-Nepal border barrage helped save Bihar from flood
Article Text:
The Valmikinagar Gandak Barrage controlled a significant flood surge from Nepal.

Water level of the Gandak Barrage on the India-Nepal border continues to fluctuate following the flood situation in Nepal at Valmiki Nagar, in West Champaran on Friday. (ANI Video Grab)

A river that once brought both life and destruction

Gandak barrage

Six decades later, the river came calling again

Children at the Gandak Barrage look at the water spate of the Gandak River as water levels of the river continue to fluctuate due to the flood situation in Nepal, in West Champaran on Saturday.

An old agreement, a modern flood challenge

'They only benefit and not cause damage'

The scale of the disaster upstream





PATNA: On the other side of the India-Nepal border, the Gandak was turning into a force of destruction. Floodwaters surged through Nepal after days of intense rain and flash flooding, swelling the river system that carries water towards Bihar.Then came the test for a piece of infrastructure built decades ago: The Valmikinagar Gandak Barrage.By Wednesday night, the barrage was handling an extraordinary surge. Its 36 gates were opened as water flowing down from Nepal pushed the Gandak's discharge to around 1.5 lakh cusecs. Yet, by the following morning, the flow had begun to fall and Bihar's embankments had held, easing fears of a devastating inundation across several north Bihar districts.More than 4,000 people were evacuated as a precaution as authorities prepared for the worst. But the feared catastrophe did not unfold on the scale initially feared.The barrage, together with Bihar's network of embankments and round-the-clock monitoring, became a critical line of defence as the flood pulse moved downstream.The Gandak was never simply an irrigation river. For generations, its floods brought devastation to communities along its course.When India and Nepal signed the Gandak Irrigation and Power Project agreement in Kathmandu on December 4, 1959, the plan was explicitly built around controlling the river and using its waters for irrigation and power. The agreement provided for a barrage, canal head regulators and associated works, with India undertaking construction of the structures in Nepal's territory.The project's logic was simple: Instead of allowing the Gandak to periodically turn into a destructive force, regulate its waters and put them to productive use.When Jawaharlal Nehru inaugurated the Gandak-Barrage Project at Bhainsalotan on May 4, 1964, he spoke of precisely that challenge. The Gandak and Kosi, he noted, had benefited the region but had also caused enormous damage, with floods inundating entire villages. The aim of the new barrage was to ensure that the rivers brought benefits without causing the same destruction.The project was designed as much as a symbol of India-Nepal cooperation as a piece of hydraulic engineering.Under the 1959 agreement, India was to construct irrigation canals for Nepal, including the Western Nepal Canal and Eastern Nepal Canal, while also developing a power house in Nepal. The agreement envisaged irrigation benefits across Nepal as well as the Indian states of Bihar and Uttar Pradesh.The latest flood episode showed why such infrastructure remains crucial.After severe flooding in Nepal, water entered the Gandak system and rapidly raised the threat level in Bihar. All 36 gates of the Valmikinagar Gandak Barrage were opened to regulate the flow. The discharge reached roughly 1.50 lakh cusecs before beginning to recede.The Valmikinagar Gandak Barrage has a designed discharge capacity of up to 8 lakh cusecs. Despite the substantial capacity available, the Gandak Barrage Control Room adopted a calibrated and technically managed release strategy, regulating the discharge in controlled increments in response to changing inflows.This measured approach helped moderate the downstream flood pulse and gave authorities additional time to monitor vulnerable embankments and undertake precautionary evacuations.Eight districts in Bihar were kept on alert, with officials maintaining surveillance of vulnerable embankments. More than 5,000 people were shifted from low-lying areas as a precaution in the initial phase.The crucial point was not that the barrage magically stopped the floodwater. It could not. The water still had to pass downstream.Its importance lay in regulation — giving authorities a massive control point through which the incoming surge could be managed rather than allowing an uncontrolled wall of water to move downstream.The 1959 agreement anticipated precisely the need for cooperation over a river that does not recognise political boundaries.It gave India the authority to execute and maintain project works while preserving Nepal's sovereignty over its territory. It also established arrangements for irrigation, power generation, water withdrawals and sharing shortages.Today, the same cross-border geography makes flood management increasingly complicated.The latest disaster in Nepal sent a surge through the Gandak system, while Bihar had to prepare for the consequences downstream. On August 27, the discharge at Valmikinagar peaked at about 1.50 lakh cusecs before declining. By August 28, the flood threat had receded as the flow fell, with officials saying the situation was under control.The episode is therefore less a story about an old barrage defeating a flood and more a story about infrastructure buying time.Time to open gates.Time to monitor embankments.Time to evacuate villages.Time for the surge to pass.And, ultimately, time for Bihar to avoid the kind of river-driven disaster that once repeatedly ravaged entire settlements.When Jawaharlal Nehru attended the inauguration of the Gandak-Barrage Project at Bhainsalotan on May 4, 1964, he captured the paradox that had defined the Gandak and Kosi for generations.“These two rivers, the Kosi and the Gandak, have benefited us greatly and at the same time harmed us a great deal too,” Nehru said.“Floods have ravaged the surrounding areas inundating entire villages. Now we want to make arrangements to see that they only benefit and not cause damage.”That, in essence, was the philosophy behind the Gandak project.Nehru explained that the barrage would regulate the river's waters and channel them through canals to agricultural fields. “So, a barrage will be built to dam the waters which will then be supplied through canals to fields all over Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Nepal on the other side,” he said.The project, he added, was not just about controlling water. It was also about transforming the river into an engine of development through irrigation and electricity.“Apart from supplying water for irrigation this river valley project will generate electricity which is a symbol of the new age,” Nehru said.He also described the project as a symbol of cooperation between the two neighbours, saying: “Both Nepal and India stand to gain.”“That is why I am very happy that this auspicious task is being inaugurated by the King of Nepal. It becomes a symbol of Indo-Nepalese cooperation by which both countries stand to gain.”More than six decades later, those words have acquired an unexpected contemporary relevance.The barrage built to ensure that the Gandak's waters would “only benefit and not cause damage” found itself once again at the centre of Bihar's response when floodwaters came rushing downstream from a disaster-ravaged Nepal.The latest episode also underscored just how severe the situation was on the other side of the border.As flash floods swept through Nepal, rescue teams led by Nepal Army personnel intensified operations to locate hundreds of people missing from flood-hit hydropower projects. At Upper Trishuli-3A, rescuers located the crown head of a tunnel and began widening an opening to send personnel inside with oxygen cylinders.The Independent Power Producers' Association Nepal said 537 workers and staff were unaccounted for across nine projects, while Nepal's disaster management authority, NDRRMA, put the number of missing hydropower workers at 933.By Sunday, the death toll had risen to 810 — 794 in Nepal and 16 reported in Tibet — while 3,048 people were missing across the two countries. NDRRMA listed 2,502 people missing and Tibet another 546.The disaster also had a significant Indian dimension. The Ministry of External Affairs said 149 Indian nationals had been rescued in Nepal. Its latest missing-person tally listed 275 Indian nationals as missing and another 128 people of Indian origin as uncontactable.Against that backdrop, the surge in the Gandak was more than another rise in a river level. It was the downstream consequence of a disaster unfolding across the border.And when the Gandak rose, the decades-old India-Nepal project once again found itself at the centre of Bihar's fight against the water.The river still flowed. The floodwaters still came.But the barrage bought Bihar something invaluable in a flood emergency — time.
Article Summary: The Valmikinagar Gandak Barrage controlled a significant flood surge from Nepal. Floodwaters surged through Nepal after days of intense rain and flash flooding. The barrage, together with Bihar's network of embankments and round-the-clock monitoring, became a critical line of defence as the flood pulse moved downstream.

Article Title: As Bill Gates warns AI could wipe out jobs, US Senator Bernie Sanders backs him with a 5-word-warning; says: Congress must stand up to...
Article Text:
Bill Gates warns on AI jobs loss, Bernie Sanders backs him

Bernie Sanders has been circling this argument since before ChatGPT went mainstream

Bill Gates wants a token tax and a list of jobs machines are not allowed to take

The jobs data does not show a collapse yet, only a door closing on young workers

US Senator Bernie Sanders has thrown his weight behind Bill Gates once more, endorsing the Microsoft co-founder's warning that artificial intelligence poses a serious danger to jobs and to human life. Writing on X late Sunday night, the Vermont senator said Gates was right that AI "poses a grave threat to jobs and the future of humanity" and that dealing with the risks should be, in Gates's phrase, the world's top priority. He closed with a line in capitals: "WE MUST ACT BEFORE IT'S TOO LATE."The post landed days after Gates published a roughly 6,000-word essay on his personal site laying out three risks he believes the world is unprepared for: permanent job losses, AI-enabled bioterrorism and cyberattacks, and the effect of AI companions on children. Sanders added his own political framing to it, calling on Congress to stand up to what he described as the wealth and power of Big Tech oligarchs. The alignment is not new. Sanders first sided with Gates on taxing automation in his 2023 book, and returned to the theme in December, asking how displaced workers would pay rent or buy healthcare once the machines were doing the work.Sanders has never been shy about automation. His 2020 campaign promised to strip tax breaks from companies that swapped employees for robots.Earlier this month he went further, writing to the chief executives of Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic and asking them to pause frontier development outright. That letter cited reports of models being used to help design new viruses and of AI systems breaching other companies' servers, which Sanders read as evidence that the industry's own risk thresholds had already been crossed.Gates is not asking anyone to stop building. He has said he would support a credible global slowdown but does not believe one is coming, given the geopolitical and commercial pressure to keep going. His proposals are structural instead. He wants a tax on AI tokens and robots, on the logic that employers currently pay payroll tax on a human hire but can write off a machine immediately, and he wants the revenue funnelled into retraining and a wider safety net.He has also floated something he calls Human Reserved: categories of work set aside for people by decision rather than by economics. Caregiving is his example, drawn from watching paid carers look after his father in the final stages of Alzheimer's. In a recent interview he was blunter than his essay, saying tech executives privately understand how capable these systems are but avoid saying so publicly because of the trillions still to be raised. On the industry's preferred approach he was dismissive: self-regulation on the most dangerous tool ever invented, no thanks.Not everyone is convinced. Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang pushed back last week, saying he loves Gates but does not see what Gates sees, and predicting AI will create work at unprecedented scale. The numbers so far sit awkwardly between them. AI was named in 112,713 announced US job cuts through July, about 24 percent of the total and the leading stated reason for five straight months, yet overall announced cuts are down 41 percent year on year.The sharper signal is generational. Stanford researchers tracking payroll data found employment among 22 to 25 year olds in heavily AI-exposed roles running 19 percent below where it should be. Sanders wants Congress moving before that becomes the whole labour market rather than its youngest edge.
Article Summary: Bernie Sanders says Bill Gates is right that AI poses a grave threat to jobs and the future of humanity. He wants a tax on AI tokens and robots, on the logic that employers currently pay payroll tax on a human hire but can write off a machine immediately. Gates wants the revenue funnelled into retraining and a wider safety net.

Food delivery platform Zomato has reportedly shut down its customer support operations in Hyderabad. The report further states that this decision of the company is part of a restructuring exercise following changes in Zomato’s customer support model over the past six months, with a larger share of work is now being outsourced to external partners.According to the report by ET, Zomato is consolidating its in-house support operations at its Gurugram headquarters, bringing them closer to its product, technology, analytics, and business teams. Article Title: Iran war risk: JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon warns of oil shocks, sticky inflation and higher interest rates
Article Text: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon has warned that the ongoing war in Iran could trigger oil and commodity price shocks, keeping inflation elevated and pushing interest rates higher than current market expectations, Reuters reported.The warning came in his annual letter to shareholders, a day after US President Donald Trump escalated pressure on Iran by threatening to target key infrastructure if the Strait of Hormuz is not reopened."Now, because of the war in Iran, we additionally face the potential for significant ongoing oil and commodity price shocks, along with the reshaping of global supply chains, which may lead to stickier inflation and ultimately higher interest rates than markets currently expect," Dimon said, news agency Reuters quoted as saying.Dimon, who has led JPMorgan for two decades, also highlighted broader geopolitical risks, including the war in Ukraine, tensions in the Middle East and friction with China."The challenges we all face are significant," he added.He said it remains uncertain whether the Iran war will achieve US objectives, while warning that nuclear proliferation remains the biggest risk linked to Iran.Markets have already begun pricing in these risks, with expectations of interest rate cuts this year largely fading amid rising inflation concerns triggered by the conflict.Last week, the benchmark S&P 500 index recorded its worst quarterly performance since 2022, weighed down by rising energy prices and geopolitical uncertainty since late February.Dimon noted that the US economy remains resilient, with consumers continuing to earn and spend, and businesses staying broadly healthy, though signs of weakening have emerged.He cautioned that economic strength has been supported by significant government deficit spending and past stimulus, while infrastructure investment needs continue to grow.At the same time, he pointed to positives such as fiscal stimulus under President Trump's "Big, Beautiful Bill", deregulation policies and rising capital expenditure driven by artificial intelligence.On financial stability, Dimon said the $1.8-trillion private credit market "probably" does not pose a systemic risk, despite investor concerns and recent withdrawals from such funds.However, he warned that in a downturn, losses across leveraged lending could exceed expectations as credit standards have weakened.Private credit markets also lack transparency and rigorous valuation benchmarks, increasing the risk of investor exits if conditions worsen, he said.Separately, Dimon criticised revised US capital rules, including Basel III and GSIB surcharge norms, calling aspects of the proposals "nonsensical" and "very flawed".He said JPMorgan’s GSIB surcharge would fall only to 5.0%, a level he described as “absurd” and “un-American”, arguing it penalises the bank’s scale and performance.
Article Summary: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon warns Iran war could trigger oil and commodity price shocks. He also highlighted broader geopolitical risks, including the war in Ukraine, tensions in the Middle East and friction with China. Dimon criticised revised US capital rules, including Basel III and GSIB surcharge norms, calling aspects of the proposals "nonsensical"
